content: If a woman becomes ill, delivers prematurely, or experiences the death of her baby, it can have significant health implications. Women who have had gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia are at an increased risk of developing hypertension, stroke, and ischemic heart disease later in life. However, it is unclear whether this is due to a shared underlying pathway or if pre-eclampsia itself increases the risk. For infants, pre-eclampsia is associated with up to 12% of cases of being born small for gestational age and 19% of preterm births. These children are at a higher risk of developmental delays and chronic health issues during childhood. The exact cause of pre-eclampsia remains unknown, and the only definitive treatment is to end the pregnancy by delivering the baby. Management strategies for pre-eclampsia aim to treat symptoms, prevent complications, and optimize the timing of delivery for the baby. Pre-eclampsia is part of a spectrum of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, which exist on a continuum with normal pregnancy. During a normal pregnancy, significant maternal physiological adaptations occur to support the growing fetus and placenta. For instance, cardiac output increases by approximately 40% in the first trimester, while blood pressure typically decreases slightly in the second trimester before returning to pre-pregnancy levels by term. Cardiac output is influenced by peripheral resistance and blood pressure, and during normal pregnancy, peripheral resistance decreases as cardiac output increases. Renal function also changes during pregnancy, with increased protein excretion, particularly in the third trimester. Protein excretion of up to 300 mg in 24 hours is considered normal in pregnancy. The classification and definition of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy have historically been controversial. However, there has been a recent consensus on standard definitions relevant to clinical practice. Hypertension in pregnancy is generally defined as a systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mmHg, a diastolic blood pressure of at least 90 mmHg, or both. Any rise in blood pressure should be confirmed by a second measurement, ideally taken at least four hours later. Automated blood pressure monitors tend to underestimate blood pressure in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia, so they should be regularly calibrated against a mercury sphygmomanometer. Proteinuria during pregnancy is defined as 300 mg or more of protein in 24 hours. In a single midstream urine sample, this corresponds to 30 mg/dL, 1+ or more on a dipstick, or a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio of at least 30 mg/mmol. Four main categories of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy are widely recognized: 1. Gestational Hypertension: Hypertension detected for the first time after 20 weeks of gestation without proteinuria, which resolves within three months of birth. 2. Pre-eclampsia: Hypertension and proteinuria detected for the first time after 20 weeks of gestation. 3. Eclampsia: The occurrence of seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia. 4. Chronic Hypertension: Hypertension known to be present before pregnancy or detected before 20 weeks of gestation. Chronic hypertension may be essential (with no underlying cause) or secondary (due to conditions such as renal, cardiac, or endocrine disease). Gestational hypertension that does not resolve after birth should be reclassified as chronic hypertension. Women with chronic hypertension may develop superimposed pre-eclampsia, diagnosed by the new onset of proteinuria, sudden worsening of hypertension or proteinuria, or the development of other signs and symptoms of pre-eclampsia after 20 weeks of gestation. Despite advances in understanding the pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia, its underlying cause remains unclear. Factors that may contribute include maternal age, parity, obesity, immune response, genetic predisposition, and pre-existing vascular diseases such as diabetes, chronic hypertension, and autoimmune conditions. Diet and nutrition may also play a role. Whether an individual woman develops pre-eclampsia likely depends on the combination and interaction of these factors. Pre-eclampsia is thought to result from inadequate blood supply to the placenta, either due to abnormal implantation or increased placental demand, such as in multiple pregnancies. Although pre-eclampsia is typically diagnosed in the second half of pregnancy, its antecedents are present much earlier. Current understanding suggests that inadequate placental blood supply leads to the release of unknown factors into the maternal circulation, which activate or injure endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial dysfunction. Endothelial dysfunction causes widespread vasoconstriction, platelet activation, and coagulation system activation. Damaged endothelial cells allow fluid to leak out of blood vessels into surrounding tissues, causing edema and reducing circulating blood volume. This leads to inadequate blood flow to many maternal organs, particularly the kidneys, liver, and brain. The vasoconstriction, microclots, and reduced circulating blood volume result in the clinical manifestations of pre-eclampsia. For a more detailed review of the etiology and pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia, refer to Meher (2005). Prevention of pre-eclampsia is discussed in detail in the generic protocol for interventions to prevent pre-eclampsia (Meher 2005). Screening for women at risk of pre-eclampsia is an essential part of antenatal care and is based on clinical history and examination. Various diagnostic tests have been proposed to identify women at high risk of developing pre-eclampsia, but none have proven to be of good predictive value and are not recommended for clinical practice. Current prevention strategies for pre-eclampsia broadly include antenatal surveillance and lifestyle modifications.
